lessons.plain: A transaction is one complete job, such as moving money between accounts. ACID describes its promises; logs and recovery help make a committed job durable and an incomplete job atomic.
goals: Define transactions and explain the ACID promises
Read active, committed, failed, and aborted states
Explain how logs help implement atomicity and durability

topics.title: Transaction
topics.definition: A transaction is a sequence of database operations treated as one logical unit of work.
details: A transaction may read or write several values. The DBMS should not leave only half of the intended result.
COMMIT makes successful changes final. ROLLBACK cancels a failed transaction's changes.
topics.example: A transfer from account A to B is one transaction even though it updates two rows.

topics.title: The four ACID promises
topics.definition: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.
details: Atomicity: all operations happen or none do. Consistency: a correct transaction preserves declared rules. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not produce an invalid combined result.
Durability: once committed, a result survives a crash. Logging and recovery support atomicity and durability; concurrency control supports isolation.
topics.example: If a transfer debits A and credits B, A+B should remain the same. A crash after only the debit must not leave money missing.

topics.title: Transaction states
topics.definition: A transaction moves from active work toward commit, or from failure toward abort.
details: A common state diagram includes Active, Partially Committed, Committed, Failed, Aborted, and Terminated.
After the last statement, the transaction is partially committed while final checks and log actions complete. It may then commit, or a failure may move it to Failed and then Aborted.
topics.example: A transaction that cannot satisfy a constraint may fail before commit and be rolled back.

topics.title: Implementation of atomicity and durability
topics.definition: Atomicity means a transaction takes effect completely or not at all. Durability means a committed result survives a crash.
details: A common method uses a log. Before a changed data page is written, its log record is made stable (write-ahead logging). The log stores enough information to undo an unfinished change or redo committed work.

After a crash, recovery undoes transactions that did not commit and redoes committed updates that were not copied to their data pages. The system confirms commit only after its required durable log record is safe.
Some systems also teach shadow paging: write changed pages separately and switch the database root pointer at commit. This is an alternative idea; logging is common in database systems.
topics.example: A transfer moves 20 from A to B. If the machine crashes after subtracting 20 from A but before adding it to B, recovery undoes the debit unless the transaction had committed. If commit was recorded but a page was not flushed, recovery redoes the missing update.

worked.title: Move 10 points between two accounts
worked.setup: Account A has 50 points and account B has 20. Move 10 points from A to B.

steps.title: Read both accounts
steps.body: The transaction checks that A has 50 and B has 20.

steps.title: Make both changes
steps.body: Subtract 10 from A and add 10 to B. If one change fails, undo the other so points are not lost.

steps.title: Save the completed transfer
steps.body: When both changes are correct, the transaction commits. A later crash must not erase this saved transfer.

worked.answer: Atomicity means both changes happen or neither happens. Durability means a committed change stays saved. The total remains 70.

diagram.title: A transaction can commit or abort
diagram.caption: The DBMS records a final outcome only after the work has been checked.

lessons.exam: Define transaction and ACID. Draw the state diagram and explain how a transaction reaches commit or abort.

lessons.plain: A schedule is the order in which transactions' reads and writes happen. Interleaving can save time, but conflicting operations need a safe order.
goals: Read a schedule while preserving transaction order
Identify read-write, write-read, and write-write conflicts
Explain why concurrent execution needs control

topics.title: Serial and concurrent schedules
topics.definition: A schedule lists operations from one or more transactions. A serial schedule runs one whole transaction before another; a concurrent schedule interleaves their operations.
details: A valid schedule preserves the original order of operations within each transaction.
Interleaving can keep CPU and storage busy while another transaction waits, improving throughput.
topics.example: T1: read A, write A. T2: read B, write B. A schedule may interleave those steps because the transactions use different data.

topics.title: When do operations conflict?
topics.definition: Two operations conflict if they are from different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a write.
details: Read-read is not a conflict. Read-write, write-read, and write-write on the same item are conflicts.
The order of a conflicting pair can affect the result, so a scheduler must preserve a correct serial order.
topics.example: If T1 and T2 both write balance A, changing which write occurs last can change the final balance.

topics.title: Problems caused by uncontrolled overlap
topics.definition: Concurrency anomalies are incorrect results caused by unsafe interleaving.
details: A lost update occurs when one write overwrites another. A dirty read uses a value that may later be rolled back. An unrepeatable read gets different values on two reads in one transaction.
Concurrency-control protocols prevent or manage these effects.
topics.example: Two people each see one available seat and both enroll a student. Without coordination, the database may accept two students for the last seat.

worked.title: See how one update can be lost
worked.setup: There are 2 seats left. Two students try to reserve one seat at almost the same time.

rows: Both students read the starting value
Student A calculates a new value
Student B calculates from the same old value
Both write 1; the last write replaces the other

steps.title: Both see the same number
steps.body: Each booking reads 2 seats before either booking saves its change.

steps.title: Both calculate one seat left
steps.body: Each subtracts one from 2, so each prepares to write 1.

steps.title: One booking overwrites the other
steps.body: The final value is 1, even though two seats were booked. One update disappeared: a lost update.

worked.answer: The correct value is 0 seats. The DBMS must coordinate the two bookings so one cannot overwrite the other's change.

diagram.title: Two transactions touch the same value
diagram.caption: The overlapping writes can overwrite a change unless the DBMS controls their order.

lessons.exam: Define serial and concurrent schedules. Identify conflicting operation pairs and explain the motivation for concurrency control.

lessons.plain: Serializability asks whether an interleaved schedule gives the same result as some safe serial order. A precedence graph turns that question into a cycle check.
goals: Build a precedence graph from conflicting operations
Test for a cycle and read a serial order from an acyclic graph
Distinguish conflict serializability from view serializability

topics.title: Conflict serializability
topics.definition: A schedule is conflict-serializable if swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations can turn it into a serial schedule.
details: Create one graph node for each transaction. For each conflict on the same item, draw an arrow from the transaction with the earlier operation to the one with the later operation.
If the graph has no directed cycle, the schedule is conflict-serializable. A topological ordering gives an equivalent serial order.
topics.example: T1 writes A before T2 reads A, so draw T1→T2.

topics.title: Cycles in the precedence graph
topics.definition: A directed cycle means the transactions require contradictory orders, so the schedule is not conflict-serializable.
details: One edge T1→T2 says T1 must come before T2. A reverse edge T2→T1 says the opposite.
The cycle test applies to conflict serializability, not every other notion of equivalence.
topics.example: T1→T2 and T2→T1 form a cycle, so no serial order can satisfy both.

topics.title: View serializability
topics.definition: View equivalence preserves which transaction each read gets its value from and which transaction performs the final write.
details: View serializability includes every conflict-serializable schedule and may include some additional schedules with blind writes.
A blind write does not first read the value it overwrites. This can make view-equivalent schedules harder to check than the graph test.
topics.example: For an exam answer, state the reads-from and final-writer conditions rather than treating view serializability as just another name for the conflict graph.

topics.title: Testing a schedule for serializability
topics.definition: The precedence-graph test decides conflict serializability by turning conflicting operation order into directed edges between transactions.
details: Write one node for each transaction. Compare operations from different transactions on the same item; a pair conflicts when at least one operation is a write.
For each conflict, draw an edge from the transaction whose operation happens first to the one whose operation happens later. Ignore read-read pairs.
If the graph is acyclic, a topological order gives an equivalent serial order. If it contains a cycle, the schedule is not conflict-serializable.
topics.example: For S = r1(X), w1(X), r2(X), w2(Y), r1(Y), the conflict on X gives T1→T2; the conflict on Y gives T2→T1. The cycle T1→T2→T1 means S is not conflict-serializable.

worked.title: Use arrows to test a schedule
worked.setup: Two transactions change two marks, A and B. The order is T1 changes A, T2 reads A, T2 changes B, then T1 changes B.

rows: T1 acts before T2 on A
T2 acts before T1 on B

steps.title: Draw the first arrow
steps.body: T1 changes A before T2 reads A. To keep this order, T1 must come before T2.

steps.title: Draw the second arrow
steps.body: T2 changes B before T1 changes B. To keep this order, T2 must come before T1.

steps.title: Look for a loop
steps.body: The arrows say T1 before T2 and T2 before T1. That is a cycle, so no single serial order can match it.

worked.answer: A cycle in the conflict graph means this schedule is not conflict-serializable.

diagram.title: The precedence graph
diagram.caption: An acyclic graph is conflict-serializable; a cycle is not.

lessons.exam: Construct the precedence graph for a schedule, test it for a cycle, and compare conflict and view serializability.

lessons.plain: Recoverability is about commit order after a read. Cascadeless and strict schedules add stronger rules that make failures easier to handle.
goals: Classify recoverable, cascadeless, and strict schedules
Explain the implication between the three

topics.title: Recoverable schedule
topics.definition: If T2 reads a value written by T1, a recoverable schedule makes T2 commit only after T1 commits.
details: If T1 aborts, T2 must still be allowed to roll back before its own commit.
Recoverability protects committed results from depending on work that may be undone.
topics.example: T1 writes A; T2 reads A; T1 commits; then T2 commits. This order is recoverable.

topics.title: Cascadeless schedule
topics.definition: A cascadeless schedule allows a transaction to read a value only after the transaction that wrote it has committed.
details: This prevents dirty reads and avoids a chain of dependent transactions all needing to abort.
It is stricter than recoverability because it delays the read itself, not just the reader's commit.
topics.example: If T1 has written A but not committed, T2 waits before reading A.

topics.title: Strict schedule
topics.definition: A strict schedule prevents other transactions from reading or writing an item that a transaction has written but not yet committed or aborted.
details: The waiting rule protects both reads and overwrites of uncommitted values.
Strictness makes undo simpler because an uncommitted value has not escaped to another transaction.
topics.example: After T1 writes A, both T2's read(A) and write(A) wait until T1 finishes.

worked.title: Spot a decision based on an unconfirmed payment
worked.setup: T1 records that Asha paid her fee, but has not finished. T2 sees “Paid” and issues Asha a hall ticket. Then T1 fails and the payment is cancelled.

rows: T2 reads the status and commits

steps.title: Notice the unconfirmed change
steps.body: T1 marked the fee as paid, but it has not committed. The DBMS may still cancel this change.

steps.title: T2 acts on that change
steps.body: T2 reads “Paid” and commits the hall-ticket decision before T1 has finished.

steps.title: T1 is cancelled
steps.body: The payment is undone, but the hall-ticket decision has already been committed using that temporary value.

worked.answer: T2 read data that was not yet confirmed. This is a dirty read, and the schedule is not recoverable because T2 committed before the transaction it depended on.

lessons.exam: Given a schedule, determine whether it is recoverable, cascadeless, or strict. Explain dirty reads and cascading rollback.
